subject: Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models

messages.author: e3e5a41ff7911cc9
messages.subject: Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models
parts:
Hi Everyone,
I have a question regarding the proper way to rank variables in terms of their effect on an outcome. Any papers, books, or ideas are welcome.

Suppose I construct a collection of bayesian models that explain an outcome. These are created by some feature selection algorithm like stepaic or glmnet with bootstraping or some other procedure. So now I have a series of stan models from which I can predict samples. By sampling from this emsemble I can get the posterior of the outcome. 

 I would like to get an idea of the importance of each of the variables involved, by perturbing each of them (by setting them to small or large values) and sample from the outcome under each condition (and for each model), and then calculate a "treatment" effect. Some perturbations may have a large effect on the outcome but with a large variance while others may have a smaller effect but with less variance. 

 What is the proper way to rank the effect of each perturbation on the outcome? I'm concerned about applying some standard statistical test because I can sample any number of samples from the model so any tiny difference in effect would be significant with enough samples.

 thanks 
FKG

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models
parts:
Why do you want to do this? If you're building something like
a regression with different predictors, then how much a predictor
adds to the mix depends on the other predictors you use and what
the prior is. There are some really neat illustrations of this in
the Hastie et al. machine learning book when they look at path
regressions (you can find it in the same diagrams in their elastic
net paper, too).

We tend to compare models by their calibration (do they get
the right posterior coverage in held out or cross-validation
tests) and their sharpeness (do they make tight predictions in
the sense of the posterior predictive intervals being narrow).
We can also evaluate more traditionally just on held-out data
likelihood.

There are a bajillion traditional methods for doing this, such
as ANOVA, many of which have Bayesian analogues.

- Bob

messages.author: e3e5a41ff7911cc9
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models
parts:
Hi Bob
thanks for taking the time to reply. 

The application I have in mind is one of causal inference with bayesian networks in biological data. Programs like bnlearns and others try to learn bayesian networks that explains the observed data. An example is to try to learn the connection between genes from observed gene expression.

Because of uncertainty in learning the structure, it is common to learn multiple Bayesian networks and see what patterns are constant. One way to accomplish this is by bootstrapping the data.

Once we have the different networks one important step is to try to figure out what perturbations (or interventions) have the largest effect on a specific outcomes. For example, if I knockdown a gene (make it have zero value. This can be accomplish in practice with certain drugs) what is the effect on some other gene of importance (a gene that is known to be associated to disease progresssion for example). Once we have the different networks we can alter the networks to simulate this type of knowdown and then sample from the network and see what happens to the gene of interest.

Anyway, I'm trying to figure out how to use Stan can help improve some of the process. Specifically, I'm trying to understand how I could rank perturbations in terms of the largest effect accounting for uncertainty and magnitude as well as the fact that we can get different estimated effects from the different networks.

thanks
Fred

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effects of perturbations of variables in ensemble of models
parts:
Stan itself only provides the Bayesian estimation or MLE point estimates.

We provide the loo package in R to do cross-validation if that's the
kind of thing you're talking about. I don't know what kind of models
you're talking about or if it's even possible to do Bayesian inference
with them --- many of the popular models for discovering network structure
or causal structure are combinatorially intractable in principle, so
need to be approximated some way in practice.

- Bob


Without specifying the kinds of modeThe kind of approaches you're talking about aren't Bayesian and
we don't have anything in Stan to do anything like what you're
talking about.
